network.overall_strategy: This is a connected, literature-guided hypothesis network, not an experimentally validated complete synthesis. The supplied literature does not establish a confirmed, regioselective abiotic route to free glutamine. Ten distinct candidate reaction sequences are represented: four glutamate-supply routes paired with two explicitly speculative activation chemistries, plus two alternative orders of selective aminodinitrile hydrolysis. These are not ten independently demonstrated syntheses. Supported precursor chemistry is separated from unresolved target-forming reactions in every reaction record. Cyanamide activation is excluded because its effectiveness cannot be assumed. Acetyl-phosphate and trimetaphosphate activation remain unvalidated alternatives, not solutions to the amidation bottleneck. Glutamine-forming experiments are restricted to cool, UV-shielded, anoxic water; pyroglutamate formation and activated-intermediate hydrolysis are included as competing sinks. Numerical literature benchmarks are distinguished from proposed screening conditions, and unreported catalyst loadings, residence times, transfer recoveries and selectivities are identified rather than invented. Feedstocks define the network boundary; their presence at useful concentrations is not established. Neutral molecular formulas represent protonation-normalized organic and phosphate pools, while redox-active metal ions and protons are explicit. Stoichiometric coefficients are omitted from input/output arrays as requested. Stereochemistry is unspecified: no enantioselective synthesis of L-glutamine is claimed. The Surface and Biochemical labels describe physical reaction settings, not evidence of biological catalysis. Cooling, sediment shielding and mineral settling do not imply removal of dissolved metals or competing nucleophiles. Net glutamine accumulation remains unestablished until production, competing reactions and transport losses are measured in realistic mixtures.

reactions.name: Copper-mediated oxidative synthesis of cyanoacetylene
agents: Cu(I)-chloride complexes in a Nieuwland-type chloride brine

conditions.temperature: Near ambient in the reported chemistry; proposed environmental window 300-310 K
conditions.pressure: Approximately 1 atm; acetylene partial pressure is not specified in the supplied report
conditions.catalyst: Cu(I)-chloride complexes; Cu(II) is a consumed oxidant, not a catalytic electron source
conditions.other: Anoxic CuCl/NaCl-KCl brine; staged HCN addition liberates cyanoacetylene from copper acetylide material. Catalyst loading, residence time and environmental Cu(II) supply are unresolved. The formal redox balance consumes two Cu(II) ions per cyanoacetylene.

reactions.mechanism: Copper-assisted cyanide-acetylene coupling removes two hydrogen equivalents, reducing Cu(II) to Cu(I); subsequent ligand/proton exchange releases cyanoacetylene.
reactions.reasoning: SUPPORTED PRECURSOR CHEMISTRY: Patel et al. (2015) report isotope-supported cyanoacetylene formation exceeding 25% under their staged laboratory conditions. This does not establish sustained Cu(II) availability on an anoxic surface. No oxygen-dependent copper regeneration is assumed, and dissolved copper carryover remains a downstream compatibility issue.

reactions.name: Hydrocyanation of cyanoacetylene to maleonitrile

conditions.other: Neutral to slightly alkaline HCN-containing water; staged delivery. Exact concentrations, residence time and numerical pH for the reported yield are not supplied in the research summary. This edge represents one branch of a product mixture, not exclusive maleonitrile production.

reactions.mechanism: Cyanide addition across the activated alkyne followed by protonation produces an unsaturated dinitrile.
reactions.reasoning: SUPPORTED PRECURSOR BRANCH: Patel et al. (2015) report maleonitrile together with cyanohydrin and, under slightly alkaline ammoniacal conditions, an additional aminonitrile. The approximately 50% maleonitrile yield is a branch-specific laboratory result and is not treated as a cascade yield.

reactions.name: Sulfide-driven photoreduction of maleonitrile

conditions.other: Anoxic aqueous sulfide with 254 nm laboratory irradiation. Photon fluence, sulfide concentration and residence time are not specified in the supplied report. Maleonitrile can photoisomerize during irradiation. S8 is an endpoint sulfur-accounting species, not a claim that it is the only immediate sulfur photoproduct.

reactions.mechanism: Photogenerated reducing equivalents hydrogenate the dinitrile carbon-carbon double bond while sulfide is oxidized toward elemental sulfur.
reactions.reasoning: SUPPORTED PRECURSOR CHEMISTRY: Patel et al. (2015) report approximately 90% succinonitrile formation. The actual solar spectrum and local sulfide supply require separate evaluation; a 254 nm laboratory result is not a measured natural-pool rate (Ranjan et al., 2018). Representing sulfur as S8 requires inferred coefficients of eight, without any conservation violation.

reactions.name: Selective photoreduction of one succinonitrile terminus

conditions.other: Further staged irradiation with sulfide; 254 nm laboratory benchmark. Irradiation duration and absorbed photon dose are not provided in the supplied summary. This stage precedes any glutamine formation.

reactions.mechanism: One nitrile is reduced to an imine-level intermediate and hydrolyzed to an aldehyde, releasing ammonia; the second nitrile remains intact.
reactions.reasoning: SUPPORTED PRECURSOR CHEMISTRY: Patel et al. (2015) report approximately 89% formation of the semialdehyde. This substrate-specific photoreduction selectivity does not establish the different nitrile-hydrolysis selectivities required to obtain glutamine. Elemental sulfur is again represented as an S8 endpoint pool.

reactions.name: Cyanohydrin formation from 3-cyanopropanal

conditions.other: HCN delivered after the photoreduction stage. No mineral catalyst is assumed. Exact reagent concentrations and equilibration time are not specified in the supplied summary.

reactions.mechanism: Cyanide attacks the aldehyde carbonyl, followed by proton transfer to form the cyanohydrin.
reactions.reasoning: SUPPORTED PRECURSOR CHEMISTRY: Patel et al. (2015) report essentially quantitative cyanohydrin formation under the investigated conditions. An achiral setting gives no demonstrated preference for the configuration needed for L-glutamine.

reactions.name: Strecker conversion to 2-aminopentanedinitrile

conditions.other: Sequential ammonia addition to the cyanohydrin-containing mixture. Exact ammoniacal concentration and reaction time are not supplied in the report. Sulfide and copper carryover are not assumed to disappear.

reactions.mechanism: Cyanohydrin-aldehyde equilibration, imine formation with ammonia and cyanide capture produce the alpha-aminodinitrile.
reactions.reasoning: SUPPORTED PRECURSOR CHEMISTRY: Patel et al. (2015) report about 70% aminodinitrile yield over the two steps from the semialdehyde. They did not demonstrate its conversion to free glutamine. This node is a validated precursor endpoint, not evidence that either subsequent selective hydrolysis route works.

reactions.name: Complete aminodinitrile hydrolysis to glutamate

conditions.temperature: Proposed screening range 333-363 K; not a reported optimization for this substrate
conditions.other: Proposed screen: pH 1-2, 1-7 days, with direct measurement of glutamate recovery and lactam formation. Four water molecules are required per dinitrile in the inferred balance. Neutralization and cooling to 300-303 K are required before activation; recovery and salt carryover are unknown.

reactions.mechanism: Both nitriles hydrolyze through amides to carboxylic acids, releasing two ammonia equivalents in protonation-normalized bookkeeping.
reactions.reasoning: CHEMICALLY PLAUSIBLE BUT UNVALIDATED FOR THIS PRECURSOR UNDER THE PROPOSED CONDITIONS: Patel et al. (2015) establish the aminodinitrile, not this hydrolysis and recovery sequence. Complete nitrile hydrolysis is standard chemistry, but pyroglutamate formation and other losses must be quantified. The proposed conditions must not be applied to glutamine itself.

reactions.name: Hydrogen-driven assembly of the alpha-ketoglutarate skeleton

conditions.catalyst: Metallic nickel; loading and surface preparation are not specified in the supplied report
conditions.other: Abiotic, anoxic, gas-pressurized water-filled pores rather than an open atmospheric pool. Near-neutral conditions are literature-guided. This is a net multistep carbon-skeleton assembly edge. Substrate concentrations, individual intermediate kinetics, catalyst loading and residence time must be recovered from the primary experimental protocol before implementation.

reactions.mechanism: Net aldol-based coupling of glyoxylate and pyruvate, coupled to hydrogen-dependent reduction/deoxygenation, generates alpha-ketoglutarate.
reactions.reasoning: LITERATURE-SUPPORTED NET PRECURSOR MODULE: Kaur et al. (2024), as summarized in the supplied report, connect hydrogen-driven carbon-skeleton assembly with alpha-ketoglutarate production. The node does not assert a single elementary reaction or an independently demonstrated concentrated alpha-ketoglutarate reservoir. This is not the distinct metal-free network of Stubbs et al. (2020).

reactions.name: Nickel-catalyzed hydrogen reductive amination

conditions.catalyst: Metallic nickel; loading is not provided in the supplied report
conditions.other: Anoxic water, pH 7-8, 6-150 mM total ammoniacal nitrogen as a reported study range. These values do not specify one optimized alpha-ketoglutarate experiment. Residence time and nickel loading remain unspecified. Depressurization and transport into a shielded surface compartment require measured recovery.

reactions.mechanism: Ammonia forms an imine or iminium species with the ketoacid, followed by nickel-mediated hydrogenation to glutamate.
reactions.reasoning: SUPPORTED GLUTAMATE FORMATION: Kaur et al. (2024) demonstrate H2-driven ketoacid reductive amination, including alpha-ketoglutarate. This supports glutamate supply only. Nickel carryover, competing hydrogenation and ketoacid availability remain relevant, and reductive-amination kinetics depend on the reducing system rather than universally favoring alpha-ketoglutarate (Mayer and Moran, 2022).

reactions.name: Iron-driven hydroxylamine reductive amination

conditions.other: Native iron is a consumed reductant, not an unspecified catalyst. The formal balance requires two Fe atoms and four protons per glutamate. Exact pH, iron surface area, hydroxylamine concentration and residence time are not supplied in the report. Cooling alone does not remove dissolved Fe(II) or residual hydroxylamine.

reactions.mechanism: Hydroxylamine forms an oxime, which is reduced to the amino acid by oxidation of metallic iron.
reactions.reasoning: SUPPORTED PRECURSOR FRAMEWORK WITH INCOMPLETE OPERATING DETAIL: Muchowska et al. (2019) report iron/hydroxylamine chemistry producing glutamate at 70 degrees Celsius. The balanced net edge does not establish its rate at an arbitrary pH. Hydroxylamine supply is a boundary assumption, and residual hydroxylamine can intercept subsequently activated glutamate as hydroxamates.

reactions.name: Aluminium-assisted transamination from glycine
agents: Dissolved aluminium species supplied experimentally as potassium alum

conditions.catalyst: Potassium alum, AlK(SO4)2, reported at 0.1 equivalent
conditions.other: Reported benchmark: pH 5, 350 mM glycine, 1.2 equivalents alpha-ketoglutarate and 4 h residence time. Aluminium hydrolysis and mineral availability require geochemical assessment. The stream must cool to 300-303 K before any glutamine-forming step; residual glycine remains a competing nucleophile.

reactions.mechanism: Aluminium-assisted imine chemistry transfers the amino group from glycine to alpha-ketoglutarate, producing glutamate and glyoxylate.
reactions.reasoning: SUPPORTED GLUTAMATE FORMATION: The supplied account of Stubbs et al. (2020) reports approximately 44% glutamate under these concentrated transamination conditions. The metal-free description of their carbon network must not be extended to this aluminium-assisted step. This route uses rxn_008 for carbon-skeleton supply and does not misidentify that upstream reaction as metal-free.

reactions.name: Hypothesized gamma-carboxyl phosphorylation by acetyl phosphate

conditions.other: Proposed, not validated: anoxic UV-shielded water at pH 7.0-7.5; 1-5 mM glutamate and 5-50 mM acetyl phosphate; sample from minutes through 24 h. These concentrations are screening choices, not demonstrated environmental abundances. No selective mineral catalyst or purification is assumed.

reactions.mechanism: Hypothesized attack of the gamma-carboxylate on phosphorus would transfer phosphoryl activation from acetyl phosphate to glutamate, releasing acetate.
reactions.reasoning: SPECULATIVE AND DECISIVE BOTTLENECK: No supplied study demonstrates this enzyme-free reaction or its gamma selectivity. Biological gamma-carboxyl activation provides mechanistic context only; ATP-dependent tRNA amidation is not evidence that acetyl phosphate performs this transfer (Curnow et al., 1997). Acetyl transfer, alpha-carboxyl activation and donor hydrolysis may dominate. Activation potential alone does not establish favorable transfer, useful yield or glutamine production.

reactions.name: Conditional ammonolysis of gamma-glutamyl phosphate

conditions.other: Anoxic, sediment-shielded water at pH 7.0-7.5; proposed 50-150 mM total ammoniacal nitrogen. Using pKa approximately 9.25, free NH3 is only approximately 0.28-2.6 mM across these limits. Time-resolved sampling must resolve ammonolysis, hydrolysis and cyclization; no productive residence time is known.

reactions.mechanism: Ammonia attacks the activated gamma-carbonyl, and phosphate departure would produce glutamine.
reactions.reasoning: CONDITIONAL CHEMICAL PLAUSIBILITY, NOT DEMONSTRATED PREBIOTIC SYNTHESIS: Acyl-phosphate ammonolysis has biochemical precedent, but enzyme-organized activation/ammonia delivery cannot be assumed in water (Curnow et al., 1997). The lifetime and regioidentity of mol_027 must first be established. Hydrolysis and intramolecular lactamization compete, while residual glycine or hydroxylamine can divert the intermediate. Cool conditions improve persistence but do not demonstrate production (Arii et al., 1999).

reactions.name: Hypothesized trimetaphosphate ring opening by glutamate

conditions.other: Proposed, not validated: anoxic UV-shielded concentrated water or hydrated films at pH 7.0-7.5; 1-5 mM glutamate and 5-50 mM cyclic trimetaphosphate; sample over minutes to 24 h. Natural trimetaphosphate abundance and a sufficiently rapid reaction at this pH are unresolved.

reactions.mechanism: Hypothetical gamma-carboxylate attack on cyclic trimetaphosphate opens a P-O-P linkage, giving a gamma-acyl triphosphate mixed anhydride, not directly gamma-glutamyl monophosphate.
reactions.reasoning: SPECULATIVE ALTERNATIVE ACTIVATION: No supplied paper identifies this glutamate-derived intermediate or demonstrates glutamine formation from it. It is included as a falsifiable polyphosphate-activation hypothesis, not as an established replacement for ATP. Alpha-amine phosphorylation, alpha-carboxyl activation and phosphate hydrolysis may dominate. Its distinction from rxn_012 is a different donor and different proposed activated intermediate, not merely a different environment.

reactions.name: Conditional ammonolysis of gamma-glutamyl triphosphate

conditions.other: UV-shielded anoxic water, pH 7.0-7.5; proposed 50-150 mM total ammoniacal nitrogen, corresponding approximately to 0.28-2.6 mM NH3. Establish mol_030 structurally before interpreting this reaction. Formation rates and allowable residence time are unknown.

reactions.mechanism: If the gamma-acyl triphosphate exists, ammonia could attack its acyl carbonyl and displace linear triphosphate.
reactions.reasoning: SPECULATIVE, CONDITIONAL ON AN UNOBSERVED INTERMEDIATE: No supplied reaction-specific study supports free glutamine production through this species. Attack at phosphorus, deactivation by water and intramolecular attack by glutamate's alpha-amine are alternatives. This branch must be tested against rxn_026 and rxn_027, not credited as productive merely because its net equation balances.

reactions.name: Hypothesized alpha-nitrile hydrolysis with side-chain nitrile retention

conditions.other: Anoxic dark water; pH 7-10 screening with time points from hours to 11 days. This is a precursor stage, not a glutamine accumulation stage. Any alkaline aliquot must be adjusted to pH 7.0-7.5 before rxn_017. No established catalyst or selective operating window exists for this unprotected C5 substrate.

reactions.mechanism: The alpha-nitrile would have to pass through an alpha-amide to the carboxylic acid while the terminal side-chain nitrile remains unreacted.
reactions.reasoning: SPECULATIVE REGIOSELECTIVITY: Green et al. (2023) found differential nitrile hydration in N-formyl substrates, including a shorter-chain analogue at pH 10 and 313 K over 11 days. That result neither demonstrates full alpha-amide-to-acid hydrolysis nor validates this unprotected C5 substrate. Patel et al. (2015) provide the precursor only. Alpha-amide accumulation and cyclization are unresolved competitors.

reactions.name: Hypothesized side-chain nitrile hydration to glutamine

conditions.other: Anoxic UV-shielded water, pH 7.0-7.5. No mineral, metal or uncatalyzed rate is established. Sample on a minutes-to-days schedule while measuring both nitrile disappearance and glutamine loss. Formation may be too slow for accumulation.

reactions.mechanism: One water molecule hydrates the remaining nitrile to a primary amide, with reaction stopping before further hydrolysis to glutamate.
reactions.reasoning: SPECULATIVE TARGET-FORMING BOTTLENECK: Neither Patel et al. (2015) nor Green et al. (2023) demonstrates this reaction at glutamine-compatible conditions. A useful hydration rate and amide endpoint cannot be inferred from stoichiometry. Glutamine requires chromatographic distinction from isoglutamine and orthogonal structural confirmation, rather than exact mass alone.

reactions.name: Hypothesized side-chain-first hydration of the aminodinitrile

conditions.other: Anoxic UV-shielded water, pH 7.0-7.5. No selective catalyst is known from the supplied literature. This is a low-priority selectivity test; no reaction time or yield can be assigned.

reactions.mechanism: The side-chain nitrile would hydrate to an amide while retaining the alpha-aminonitrile.
reactions.reasoning: SPECULATIVE AND LESS SUPPORTED THAN THE ALPHA-FIRST ORDER: Patel et al. (2015) did not perform this hydration. Related protected-substrate observations in Green et al. (2023) favor initial alpha-nitrile reaction rather than the selectivity required here, although they do not definitively determine the unprotected C5 chemistry. This pathway is retained as a falsifiable alternative, not promoted as a demonstrated or high-confidence route.

reactions.name: Hypothesized alpha-nitrile hydrolysis while preserving the gamma-amide

conditions.other: Anoxic UV-shielded water, pH 7.0-7.5. Complete alpha-nitrile-to-acid conversion must occur without gamma-amide hydrolysis. No catalyst, residence time or kinetic selectivity has been established.

reactions.mechanism: Sequential hydration and hydrolysis of the alpha-nitrile would generate the alpha-carboxyl group while preserving the pre-existing side-chain amide.
reactions.reasoning: SPECULATIVE TARGET-FORMING BOTTLENECK: The provided literature offers no demonstration of this double selectivity. Green et al. (2023) supply only indirect, substrate-dependent hydration evidence. Conditions vigorous enough to hydrolyze the alpha-amide may also destroy the desired gamma-amide; mild conditions may simply fail to react.

reactions.name: Competing partial hydrolysis to isoglutamine

conditions.other: Monitor throughout the nitrile-hydrolysis screens. This is a net competing branch, not a measured product distribution or a claim that isoglutamine dominates.

reactions.mechanism: Partial hydrolysis leaves the alpha position as an amide while the terminal side-chain nitrile proceeds to a carboxylic acid.
reactions.reasoning: SPECULATIVE COMPETITOR REQUIRED FOR ANALYTICAL DISCRIMINATION: The selectivity problem is highlighted by the supplied review of Patel et al. (2015) and Green et al. (2023), but isoglutamine formation from this exact substrate is not demonstrated there. Isoglutamine and glutamine have identical formulas, making the tentative mass assignment of Neish et al. (2010) insufficient to settle their identity.

reactions.name: Measured glutamine loss by cyclization to pyroglutamate

conditions.temperature: 310.15 K kinetic benchmark; network formation compartments are proposed at 300-303 K
conditions.other: At pH approximately 7.2 and 310.15 K, about 10% loss per day corresponds to first-order k approximately 0.105 day^-1 and half-life approximately 6.6 days. The reported 10% loss over 9 days at 277 K corresponds to approximately 59 days half-life. These are benchmark conversions, not rates established in the proposed reaction mixtures.

reactions.mechanism: The alpha-amino group attacks the side-chain amide carbonyl intramolecularly, forming a five-membered lactam and releasing ammonia.
reactions.reasoning: SUPPORTED MANDATORY LOSS: Tritsch and Moore (1962) and Arii et al. (1999) establish glutamine instability and maximal stability around pH 5.0-7.5. Reported activation energies of approximately 48.5 and 98.7 kJ/mol come from different studies and must not be combined into a supposedly validated universal Arrhenius model. Production must exceed this loss plus transport and other chemical losses for accumulation.

reactions.name: Competing glutamine deamidation to glutamate

conditions.other: Rate depends on temperature, pH and matrix. No independent hydrolysis rate constant is assigned for 300-303 K, and this edge must not be added to rxn_021 as though both rates were separately measured by the same stability experiment.

reactions.mechanism: Hydrolysis of the side-chain amide gives glutamate and ammonia.
reactions.reasoning: SUPPORTED LOSS CLASS, UNQUANTIFIED UNDER THE PROPOSED FINAL CONDITIONS: Airaudo et al. (1987) describe glutamine conversion to glutamate during heating, followed by pyroglutamate formation under relevant conditions. This edge also explains why hot or strongly acidic analytical workups cannot establish an original glutamine concentration.

reactions.name: Thermal or concentration-assisted glutamate lactamization

conditions.temperature: Proposed monitoring window 333-370 K during precursor processing
conditions.other: Monitor during heated hydrolysis, concentration and wet-dry processing. No rapid conversion is assumed in cool dilute water, and no rate constant is assigned within this temperature window.

reactions.mechanism: Intramolecular condensation between the alpha-amino group and gamma-carboxyl group eliminates water and forms a five-membered lactam.
reactions.reasoning: SUPPORTED COMPETING CHEMISTRY WITH CONDITION-DEPENDENT KINETICS: Gayte-Sorbier et al. (1985) found that heating glutamic acid or monosodium glutamate gives pyroglutamate rather than glutamine. Much higher-temperature dry decomposition described by Weiss et al. (2018) must not be mistaken for evidence of fast lactamization in a cool prebiotic pool.

reactions.name: Hydrolytic loss of gamma-glutamyl phosphate

conditions.other: Same pH 7.0-7.5 compartment as ammonolysis. Lifetime and metal-ion effects are unknown and must be measured on a structurally confirmed intermediate.

reactions.mechanism: Water hydrolyzes the mixed carboxylic-phosphoric anhydride, returning glutamate and orthophosphate.
reactions.reasoning: CHEMICALLY EXPECTED CONDITIONAL SINK; PREBIOTIC KINETICS ARE SPECULATIVE: Biological activation chemistry establishes why such activation must be coupled to capture, but the supplied papers do not quantify free gamma-glutamyl phosphate hydrolysis in this mixture (Curnow et al., 1997). A balanced productive edge cannot be evaluated without this competing deactivation.

reactions.name: Cyclization of gamma-glutamyl phosphate

conditions.other: pH 7.0-7.5; compare directly with ammonia capture. No cyclization rate for this free activated intermediate is supplied.

reactions.mechanism: Intramolecular attack by the alpha-amino group at the activated gamma-carbonyl ejects phosphate and forms pyroglutamate.
reactions.reasoning: SPECULATIVE RATE, STRONG MECHANISTIC COMPETITION: Five-membered-ring formation is a credible competitor once the gamma-carboxyl is activated. Glutamine and glutamate lactamization studies establish the sink structure but do not measure this activated-substrate reaction (Arii et al., 1999; Gayte-Sorbier et al., 1985). No assumption that external ammonia outcompetes it is justified.

reactions.name: Hydrolytic loss of gamma-glutamyl triphosphate

conditions.other: pH 7.0-7.5; hydrolysis at the acyl linkage is represented. Other phosphate-chain cleavage reactions are possible but are not assigned unmeasured rates.

reactions.mechanism: Hydrolysis of the proposed acyl-phosphate linkage regenerates glutamate and linear triphosphate.
reactions.reasoning: SPECULATIVE CONDITIONAL SINK: No supplied study characterizes mol_030 or measures its lifetime. If it forms, water competes with ammonia for the activated acyl group. This branch is included to prevent treating an unobserved activated intermediate as quantitatively available for glutamine synthesis.

reactions.name: Cyclization of gamma-glutamyl triphosphate

conditions.other: pH 7.0-7.5; rate and intermediate abundance are unmeasured.

reactions.mechanism: The alpha-amino group attacks the proposed activated gamma-carbonyl, producing pyroglutamate and displacing triphosphate.
reactions.reasoning: SPECULATIVE CONDITIONAL SINK: Intramolecular lactamization is chemically credible but unmeasured for this hypothetical substrate. Known pyroglutamate formation motivates monitoring, not a numerical rate assignment (Gayte-Sorbier et al., 1985; Arii et al., 1999).

reactions.name: Competing acetyl phosphate hydrolysis

conditions.other: pH 7.0-7.5; monitor donor depletion with and without glutamate. Metal carryover can change hydrolysis behavior; no donor half-life is asserted.

reactions.mechanism: Water cleaves the acyl-phosphate linkage to acetate and orthophosphate.
reactions.reasoning: ESTABLISHED REACTION CLASS, SPECULATIVE NETWORK KINETICS: Acyl-phosphate hydrolysis is standard chemistry, but the supplied research contains no reaction-specific kinetic study for this mixture. This sink consumes activation capacity and must be measured rather than assuming every acetyl phosphate molecule activates glutamate.

reactions.name: Competing hydrolytic opening of cyclic trimetaphosphate

conditions.other: pH 7.0-7.5; quantify ring opening alongside any proposed glutamate-dependent product. No environmental lifetime or selectivity is assigned.

reactions.mechanism: Water opens one phosphoanhydride linkage in cyclic trimetaphosphate to form linear triphosphate.
reactions.reasoning: ESTABLISHED REACTION CLASS, SPECULATIVE NETWORK KINETICS: The supplied papers do not establish how rapidly this donor hydrolyzes relative to glutamate activation under the proposed conditions. Donor disappearance alone therefore cannot be interpreted as evidence for gamma-acyl triphosphate or glutamine formation.

pathways.name: Cyanosulfidic glutamate supply with acetyl-phosphate activation
pathways.description: Supported staged photochemistry reaches the aminodinitrile; complete hydrolysis is then proposed to supply glutamate. The decisive unresolved step is selective gamma activation by acetyl phosphate. Acid neutralization, cooling, glutamate recovery and copper/sulfide carryover require measurement. This is not a demonstrated glutamine synthesis.

pathways.name: Cyanosulfidic glutamate supply with trimetaphosphate activation
pathways.description: The same precursor supply is paired with a chemically distinct but unvalidated ring-opening activation hypothesis. Formation and gamma regioidentity of the proposed glutamyl triphosphate must be established before ammonolysis can be credited. Phosphate hydrolysis and alpha-amine phosphorylation may prevent productive activation.

pathways.name: Hydrogen-nickel glutamate supply with acetyl-phosphate activation
pathways.description: Hydrogen-dependent carbon assembly and nickel-catalyzed reductive amination supply glutamate under comparatively mild conditions. Transport from 5 bar H2 water into the final surface compartment is physical staging, not a new chemical reaction. Nickel carryover and the unvalidated acetyl-phosphate gamma-activation step remain unresolved.

pathways.name: Hydrogen-nickel glutamate supply with trimetaphosphate activation
pathways.description: Literature-supported glutamate production feeds an untested polyphosphate activation module. Mild precursor conditions do not establish the formation, lifetime or regioselectivity of gamma-glutamyl triphosphate. This sequence differs from P3 in both its activating donor and proposed activated intermediate.

pathways.name: Iron-hydroxylamine glutamate supply with acetyl-phosphate activation
pathways.description: Hydrogen-dependent carbon assembly is followed by the distinct iron/hydroxylamine amination module. The 343 K product stream must cool before target formation. Settling iron solids does not remove dissolved Fe(II) or hydroxylamine; residual hydroxylamine could intercept activated glutamate. Gamma phosphorylation remains unvalidated.

pathways.name: Iron-hydroxylamine glutamate supply with trimetaphosphate activation
pathways.description: The iron-generated glutamate stream feeds the hypothetical gamma-acyl triphosphate route after cooling. Neither removal of competing hydroxylamine nor selective polyphosphate activation is established. Both mixture-transfer experiments and direct intermediate identification are prerequisites to assessing glutamine formation.

pathways.name: Glycine transamination with acetyl-phosphate activation
pathways.description: Alpha-ketoglutarate from the hydrogen-driven assembly module undergoes experimentally supported aluminium-assisted transamination. After cooling from 353 K, residual concentrated glycine can compete with ammonia for any activated glutamate. Neither selective gamma activation nor a purification-free transition to glutamine production is demonstrated.

pathways.name: Glycine transamination with trimetaphosphate activation
pathways.description: Aluminium-assisted transamination supplies glutamate for the hypothetical trimetaphosphate branch. The metal-free label does not apply to either this aluminium-assisted amination or rxn_008. Glycine phosphorylation, competing condensation and unresolved aluminium speciation may divert the activating donor.

pathways.name: Alpha-acid-first selective aminodinitrile hydrolysis
pathways.description: Supported cyanosulfidic precursor formation is followed by two unvalidated selectivities: full alpha-nitrile-to-acid hydrolysis with side-chain nitrile retention, then side-chain hydration stopping at the amide. Protected shorter-chain analogue evidence motivates testing but does not validate either transformation for the unprotected C5 compound.

pathways.name: Side-chain-amide-first selective aminodinitrile hydrolysis
pathways.description: Supported precursor formation is followed by the alternative hydration order. This is a lower-support falsifiable candidate because related protected-substrate observations favor alpha-nitrile reaction rather than side-chain-first hydration. Subsequent complete alpha hydrolysis must preserve the gamma-amide. No successful catalyst, selective window or glutamine yield is known.

pathway_evaluations.feedback: Patel et al. (2015) support the upstream sequence through the aminodinitrile, and complete hydrolysis is a credible glutamate-supply step. The decisive gap is rxn_012: acetyl phosphate has not been shown to selectively generate gamma-glutamyl phosphate in this system. Ammonolysis in rxn_013 is chemically plausible if that intermediate exists, but its competition with hydrolysis and intramolecular cyclization is unresolved. Sequential precursor chemistry and cool final conditions are conceptually compatible, but the supplied representation does not specify operational conditions or transfer recoveries.
suggestions: Directly identify and quantify gamma-glutamyl phosphate, distinguishing it from alpha-carboxyl activation, amino-group modification and acetyl-transfer products.
Measure glutamine formation, activated-intermediate hydrolysis and pyroglutamate formation together across a defined pH, temperature and ammonia-concentration matrix.
Specify the copper-brine capture/liberation chemistry, sequential reagent delivery and composition of the mixture transferred into the activation module.

pathway_evaluations.feedback: The cyanosulfidic precursor sequence is supported, but the supplied literature does not demonstrate rxn_014 or rxn_015. Trimetaphosphate ring opening does not itself establish selective formation of a gamma-carboxyl mixed anhydride; amino-group phosphorylation, activation at other sites and hydrolysis must be distinguished. Ammonolysis is a reasonable conditional mechanism, not demonstrated glutamine synthesis. Compatibility between useful activation rates and cool, glutamine-preserving conditions remains unknown.
suggestions: Establish the connectivity and lifetime of mol_030 using complementary phosphorus spectroscopy and structure-resolving product analysis.
Measure gamma activation against alternative phosphorylation products and trimetaphosphate hydrolysis under the actual proposed final-stage conditions.
Determine whether ammonia capture outcompetes mixed-anhydride hydrolysis and cyclization without moving outside a glutamine-compatible pH range.

pathway_evaluations.feedback: Kaur et al. (2024) provide relevant support for hydrogen-driven carbon-skeleton assembly and nickel-catalyzed reductive amination under mild aqueous conditions. However, rxn_008 is a lumped transformation whose catalytic implementation is not specified in the reaction record. The documented glutamate chemistry does not validate acetyl-phosphate activation or subsequent selective glutamine accumulation. The mild upstream benchmark is environmentally compatible in principle, but nickel availability, hydrogen partial pressure and downstream mixture composition require specification.
suggestions: Expand rxn_008 into its supported condensation/dehydration and reduction chemistry, with the catalyst and conditions needed for each transformation.
Use the reported approximately 22 C, pH 7-8 and 5 bar hydrogen conditions as an explicit experimental benchmark rather than assuming that a generic aqueous setting reproduces them.
Test the activation module in the actual upstream product mixture, including dissolved metals and residual substrates, and quantify all major competing products.

pathway_evaluations.feedback: The hydrogen/nickel glutamate-supply module has relevant experimental precedent and can operate under relatively mild conditions. The target-forming module remains unsupported: neither selective gamma-carboxyl attack on trimetaphosphate nor productive ammonolysis of mol_030 is established. The balanced net equations identify a possible chemical sequence, but they do not establish intermediate connectivity, reaction rates or favorable partitioning toward glutamine.
suggestions: Specify the active nickel phase, hydrogen partial pressure, catalyst loading and mechanistic implementation of rxn_008.
Characterize mol_030 before assigning glutamine formation to its ammonolysis, and distinguish carboxyl activation from amino-group phosphorylation.
Measure activation and ammonolysis in metal-containing upstream mixtures, including phosphate speciation, hydrolysis and pyroglutamate production.

pathway_evaluations.feedback: The supplied research associates iron/hydroxylamine chemistry with glutamate production, including Muchowska et al. (2019). This pathway still requires the hydrogen-driven alpha-ketoglutarate-supply chemistry of rxn_008. A warmer precursor stage followed by cooling is not intrinsically inconsistent, but iron speciation, residual hydroxylamine and their effects on the activation mixture are unresolved. The principal target bottleneck remains selective acetyl-phosphate activation followed by productive ammonolysis.
suggestions: Specify the supported catalyst for rxn_008 and the temperature, pH, iron form and hydroxylamine concentration used for rxn_010.
Quantify glutamate recovery and dissolved iron/hydroxylamine carryover during cooling and transfer; mineral settling should not be treated as complete chemical purification.
Demonstrate gamma-glutamyl phosphate formation and a positive glutamine production-minus-loss balance in the transferred mixture.

pathway_evaluations.feedback: Iron-assisted glutamate production is a plausible precursor module, but it supplies no evidence for the proposed trimetaphosphate-mediated terminal chemistry. The concentration and speciation of dissolved iron can affect phosphate availability and reaction behavior after transfer. Cooling addresses thermal exposure but does not resolve those chemical compatibility questions. Selective formation and ammonolysis of the proposed gamma-glutamyl triphosphate remain unvalidated.
suggestions: Document the complete catalytic and environmental requirements for alpha-ketoglutarate assembly and iron/hydroxylamine reductive amination.
Measure phosphate speciation, metal association and soluble intermediate recovery after transfer into the final-stage environment.
Run a controlled comparison of glutamine formation, alternative phosphorylation, triphosphate hydrolysis and cyclization using authentic product standards.

pathway_evaluations.feedback: The supplied research reports alum-assisted glycine transamination producing glutamate at pH 5 and 80 C with concentrated glycine. That supports rxn_011 under defined laboratory conditions, not glutamine synthesis. This submitted pathway obtains alpha-ketoglutarate through rxn_008, so its upstream requirements should not be conflated with the separate metal-free ketoacid framework. Residual glycine and other nucleophiles can compete in the acetyl-phosphate module, whose gamma selectivity remains unestablished.
suggestions: Specify the catalyst for rxn_008 and justify the glycine concentration, soluble aluminium species and residence time required by rxn_011.
Measure the composition and recovery of the cooled transamination mixture rather than assuming selective transfer of glutamate.
Include glycine-containing and aluminium-containing controls when measuring activation, glutamine formation, acyl-transfer products and pyroglutamate.

pathway_evaluations.feedback: The glutamate-supply chemistry has literature precedent, subject to its specified catalyst and concentration requirements. Trimetaphosphate activation introduces an unresolved regioselectivity problem, especially in a mixture containing excess glycine and potentially dissolved aluminium. Neither gamma-glutamyl triphosphate formation nor selective conversion of that intermediate into free glutamine is demonstrated. The proposed cooling is physically reasonable, but downstream chemical compatibility is not established.
suggestions: Provide explicit operating conditions and catalyst assignments for the precursor module, including the hydrogen-driven rxn_008.
Quantify trimetaphosphate consumption by water, glycine and other nucleophiles alongside glutamate phosphorylation.
Resolve the structures of phosphorylated products and establish whether any gamma-activated intermediate produces glutamine faster than competing losses.

pathway_evaluations.feedback: This is the strongest provisional hypothesis because it bypasses unestablished carboxyl activation and its first selectivity requirement has limited support by analogy to preferential alpha-nitrile hydration. However, Green et al. (2023) studied different, N-formylated substrates; their results do not establish alpha-nitrile conversion all the way to carboxylate while retaining the side-chain nitrile in this C5 substrate. Subsequent side-chain hydration must also stop at glutamine under conditions where formation exceeds degradation. Neither selectivity window has been demonstrated.
suggestions: Measure substrate-specific rates for hydration and hydrolysis at both nitriles, explicitly distinguishing alpha-amide formation from complete alpha-nitrile hydrolysis.
Isolate or directly identify mol_032 and test its side-chain hydration separately before evaluating the coupled sequence.
Use non-hydrolytic analytical workups with glutamine, isoglutamine, glutamate and pyroglutamate standards, and quantify additional amide and cyclic products.

pathway_evaluations.feedback: The aminodinitrile-supply sequence is supported, but preferential side-chain hydration in rxn_018 has no direct support in the supplied evidence. The reported alpha-nitrile hydration preference in related substrates makes this ordering less supported than P9, although it does not establish impossibility for the unprotected C5 substrate. Rxn_019 then requires complete alpha-nitrile hydrolysis without destroying the existing gamma-amide or losing product through cyclization.
suggestions: Determine the actual site of initial hydration before assigning mol_033; molecular formula or accurate mass alone cannot establish regiochemistry.
Establish a condition window for alpha-nitrile hydrolysis that preserves the gamma-amide, measuring glutamine formation and degradation concurrently.
Compare both hydrolysis orders using matched conditions, authentic standards and time-resolved measurements rather than transferring selectivity assumptions between substrates.

evaluation.network_feedback: Not approved as a complete glutamine synthesis network. Structural validity is excellent: the 36 molecule nodes and 29 reaction nodes form a connected network, molecule IDs are consistent, and the deterministic check establishes conservation for every reaction. The eight coefficient-adjusted reactions are not conservation violations; coefficients of eight in the sulfur-producing reactions follow naturally from representing elemental sulfur as S8. The central weakness is chemical completion, not topology or stoichiometry. Every target-producing route depends on unvalidated regioselective activation, hydration or hydrolysis, and no route establishes glutamine formation faster than competing reactions and transport losses. Conditional ammonolysis of a genuine gamma-activated intermediate is chemically plausible, but that does not demonstrate its selective abiotic production or productive lifetime. The competing branches improve the network's chemical realism: rxn_020 represents a plausible but unquantified isoglutamine branch; rxn_021 has direct glutamine-degradation support; rxn_022 and rxn_023 are credible condition-dependent losses; and rxn_024-rxn_029 describe plausible hydrolytic or cyclization competition. Reactions involving mol_027 or mol_030 remain conditional on those intermediates actually forming. Sink inclusion does not substitute for measured kinetics, and high-confidence sink chemistry must not inflate confidence in target production. Environmental consistency is only partially established. Cool, shielded final-stage water is compatible with glutamine preservation, but the supplied reaction records lack sufficient step-specific pH, temperature, pressure, catalyst speciation and residence-time information. Ammonia protonation, activation rates and dissolved-metal or nucleophile carryover need explicit treatment. Warmer precursor stages and subsequent cooling are not intrinsically disqualifying. Literature alignment is strong in acknowledging the unresolved target-forming chemistry, degradation, analytical ambiguity and lack of a validated complete synthesis. However, the displayed reaction records do not provide reaction-linked citations, and supporting literature conditions cannot automatically be assumed to apply to the proposed mixtures. P9 is only a provisional experimental priority, not a demonstrated synthesis. Overall confidence reflects the unresolved target-forming bottlenecks rather than averaging supported precursor and sink reactions.
